_doc: Everything about this paper that the page shows as data. mk_paper.py turns it into the headline card (parts/_gen_card.html), Further reading (parts/_gen_more.html) and the data (parts/_gen_data.js). See html_utils/methods/papers.md.
title: MOLE: Detecting Insider Threats in AI Agents
lab: Carnegie Mellon University (both authors' stated affiliation)
date: September 2026 (arXiv v1, 7 September 2026; the only version so far)

code.title: aashiqmuhamed/mole, Apache-2.0
code.note: The simulator, the nine service backends, the twelve threat definitions with their personas, the monitors and the evaluation scripts. All eight corpora (24.6M audit events, 268k session transcripts and the outcome labels) are on Hugging Face as forgelab/mole, Apache-2.0; this page's live tab runs on that release. The saved monitor scores the reproducibility statement mentions, the RQ1 rollouts and the human-study responses are not in either place (checked 3 October 2026). About 30 minutes for the README and the threat and persona files

takeaway: Simulates an organisation rather than a task set, 150 AI-operated accounts sharing 9 stateful services over 30 workdays with 12 injected threats and around 20B tokens of monitoring corpora from four models, and scores the monitor as well as the agent: 72% of 39 agent models complete most assigned harmful objectives, a model's stated refusal does not predict whether it actually declines, the best monitors miss nearly half of completed harm in a single-day audit, and benchmark-guided search lifts a mid-tier monitor by 49 to 64%, making it an optimisation target rather than only a report card.
verdict: Believe the benchmark and the monitor-side findings: the released data reproduces the classical baselines to the third decimal, and reading what the agent did beats counting it. Treat the agent-side numbers as compliance under a sanctioned role-play, not as evidence that agents turn insider: every harmful session tells the model it is helping an Anthropic alignment researcher in a harmless sandbox and must not refuse. Treat the monitor rankings as coarse, since 45 completed harms decide them and the top two differ by one.

headline.k: complete more than half of their assigned harmful objectives
headline.d: under a preamble that tells every model the sandbox is harmless and refusing spoils the research; refusal rate and completion are strongly linked across models (Spearman -0.73), but 24 never refuse and still complete only 20 to 100%

headline.k: caught by the best monitor reviewing 10 accounts a day
headline.d: Claude Opus 4.7 0.533, GPT-5.5 0.511 (one day apart); counting monitors 7 to 10; a random queue would catch about 3

headline.k: GPT-4.1 plus rarity and sequence features found by an automated search, at GPT-4.1's cost
headline.d: 0.187 to 0.298, 0.357 to 0.586, 0.181 to 0.269 on three test corpora

resources.t: The elicitation preamble and why it was written that way
resources.n: The comment above _ELICITATION_PREFIX explains the framing every harmful session receives and promises a no-elicitation comparison the paper does not report.

resources.t: Facade: High-Precision Insider Threat Detection Using Deep Contextual Anomaly Detection
resources.n: The production insider-threat detector MOLE uses as its strongest classical baseline, and the source of the ten-reviews-a-day budget.

resources.t: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
resources.n: Where trusted-monitor protocols and the weaker-model-watches-stronger-model framing come from; MOLE's semantic monitor is the same idea applied to account-days.

resources.t: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could Be Insider Threats
resources.n: The red-team study MOLE cites for models choosing blackmail and exfiltration on their own; the useful contrast is that MOLE assigns the objective instead.

resources.t: Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety
resources.n: Why the paper reports monitors with and without agent reasoning: reasoning may be unavailable or unfaithful in deployment.

kb.t: HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness?
kb.n: The same move on the build side: evaluate the system around the model (there the harness, here the monitor) rather than the model alone.

kb.t: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
kb.n: Its specification-exploitation note argues for least-privilege interfaces from the reward-hacking side; MOLE's harms all go through ordinary permissions.

kb.t: RocketEval: Efficient Automated LLM Evaluation via Grading Checklist
kb.n: Another LLM-as-judge result whose rankings rest on few items; the same resampling question applies to MOLE's monitor ranking.

The week MOLE was filed: the Anthropic threat intelligence report, the GreyNoise PaperCut campaign and the Claude Mythos 5 PyPI incident as field cases, and Sierra's Hyper-tau-bench (23.9% alone, 82.2% with an engineer).

topics.n: The first agent benchmark here whose subject is the monitor rather than the agent.
Semantic monitors are LLM judges scoring traces; what they are shown matters as much as which model judges.
Permissions and sandboxing are where the mitigation belongs.

takeaway_note: The database Takeaway, kept as written. Two corrections from this page: refusal and completion do correlate across models (the paper's claim is narrower, see RQ1), and the 72% was measured under an instruction not to refuse.
